cards.text:
One of the most intriguing stories of the Russian Revolution concerns the identity of Anastasia, the youngest daughter of Czar Nicholas II. During his reign over Russia, the czar had planned to revoke many of the harsh laws established by previous czars. Some workers and peasants, however, clamored for more rapid social reform. In 1918, a group of these people known as Bolsheviks overthrew the government. On July 17 or 18, they murdered the czar and what was thought to be his entire family. Although witnesses vouched that all the members of the czar’s family had been executed, there were rumors suggesting that Anastasia had survived. Over the years, a number of women claimed to be Grand Duchess Anastasia. Perhaps the most famous claimant was Anastasia Tschaikovsky, who was also known as Anna Anderson.

In 1920, 18 months after the czar’s execution, this terrified young woman was rescued from drowning in a Berlin river. She spent two years in a hospital, where she attempted to reclaim her health and shattered mind. The doctors and nurses thought that she resembled Anastasia and questioned her about her background. She disclaimed any connection with the czar’s family.
Eight years later, however, she claimed that she was Anastasia. She said that she had been rescued by two Russian soldiers after the czar and the rest of her family had been killed. Two brothers named Tschaikovsky had carried her into Romania. She had married one of the brothers, who had taken her to Berlin and left her there, penniless and without a vocation. Unable to invoke the aid of her mother’s family in Germany, she had tried to drown herself.

During the next few years, scores of the czar’s relatives, ex-servants, and acquaintances interviewed her. Many of these people said that her looks and mannerisms were evocative of the Anastasia that they had known. Her grandmother and other relatives denied that she was the real Anastasia, however.

Tired of being accused of fraud, Anastasia immigrated to the United States in 1928 and took the name Anna Anderson. She still wished to prove that she was Anastasia, though, and returned to Germany in 1933 to bring suit against her mother’s family. There she declaimed to the court, asserting that she was indeed Anastasia and deserved her inheritance.

In 1957, the court decided that it could neither confirm nor deny Anastasia’s identity.
Although it will probably never be known whether this woman was the Grand Duchess Anastasia, her search to establish her identity has been the subject of numerous books, plays, and movies.

7:10:107:1.instruction: This idea was repellent to the Wright brothers, however, and they searched for more efficient methods to control the balance of airborne vehicles. In 1900 and 1901, the Wrights tested numerous gliders and developed control techniques. The brothers’ inability to obtain enough lift power for the gliders almost led them to abandon their efforts.

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
Many great inventions are initially greeted with ridicule and disbelief. The invention of the airplane was no exception. Although many people who heard about the first powered flight on December 17, 1903, were excited and impressed, others reacted with peals of laughter. The idea of flying an aircraft was repulsive to some people. Such people called Wilbur and Orville Wright, the inventors of the first flying machine, impulsive fools. Negative reactions, however, did not stop the Wrights. Impelled by their desire to succeed, they continued their experiments in aviation.

Orville and Wilbur Wright had always had a compelling interest in aeronautics and mechanics. As young boys, they earned money by making and selling kites and mechanical toys.
Later, they designed a newspaper-folding machine, built a printing press, and operated a bicycle- repair shop. In 1896, when they read about the death of Otto Lilienthal, the brothers’ interest in flight grew into a compulsion.

Lilienthal, a pioneer in hang-gliding, had controlled his gliders by shifting his body in the desired

After further study, the Wright brothers concluded that the published tables of air pressure on curved surfaces must be wrong. They set up a wind tunnel and began a series of experiments with model wings. Because of their efforts, the old tables were repealed in time and replaced by the first reliable figures for air pressure on curved surfaces. This work, in turn, made it possible for the brothers to design a machine that would fly. In 1903, the Wrights built their first airplane, which cost less than $1,000. They even designed and built their own source of propulsion—a lightweight gasoline engine. When they started the engine on December 17, the airplane pulsated wildly before taking off. The plane managed to stay aloft for 12 seconds, however, and it flew 120 feet.

By 1905, the Wrights had perfected the first airplane that could turn, circle, and remain airborne for half an hour at a time. Others had flown in balloons and hang gliders, but the Wright brothers were the first to build a full-size machine that could fly under its own power. As the contributors to one of the most outstanding engineering achievements in history, the Wright brothers are accurately called the fathers of aviation.

COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

choices: a. The high cost of the invention

d. Disbelief in their bicycle business success ​

cards.title: Question

c. Inspired them to copy Otto Lilienthal's designs
d. Led to immediate glider lift achievements

b. Confirmed existing air pressure tables

In the 16th century, an age of great marine and terrestrial exploration, Ferdinand Magellan led the first expedition to sail around the world. As a young Portuguese noble, he served the king of Portugal, but he became involved in the quagmire of political intrigue at court and lost the king’s favor. After he was dismissed from service by the king of Portugal, he offered to serve the future Emperor Charles V of Spain.
A papal decree of 1493 had assigned all land in the New World west of 50 degrees W longitude to Spain and all the land east of that line to Portugal. Magellan offered to prove that the East Indies fell under Spanish authority. On September 20, 1519, Magellan set sail from Spain with five ships. More than a year later, one of these ships was exploring the topography of South America in search of a water route across the continent. This ship sank, but the remaining four ships searched along the southern peninsula of South America. Finally, they found the passage they sought near 50 degrees S latitude. Magellan named this passage the Strait of All Saints, but today it is known as the Strait of Magellan.

One ship deserted while in this passage and returned to Spain, so fewer sailors were privileged to gaze at that first panorama of the Pacific Ocean. Those who remained crossed the meridian now known as the International Date Line in the early spring of 1521 after 98 days on the Pacific Ocean.
During those long days at sea, many of Magellan’s men died of starvation and disease.

Later, Magellan became involved in an insular conflict in the Philippines and was killed in a tribal battle. Only one ship and 17 sailors under the command of the Basque navigator Elcano survived to complete the westward journey to Spain and thus prove once and for all that the world is round, with no precipice at the edge.

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
Conflict had existed between Spain and England since the 1570s. England wanted a share of the wealth that Spain had been taking from the lands it had claimed in the Americas.

Elizabeth I, Queen of England, encouraged her staunch admiral of the navy, Sir Francis Drake, to raid Spanish ships and towns. Though these raids were on a small scale, Drake achieved dramatic success, adding gold and silver to England’s treasury and diminishing Spain’s supremacy.

Religious differences also caused conflict between the two countries. Whereas Spain was Roman Catholic, most of England had become Protestant. King Philip II of Spain wanted to claim the throne and make England a Catholic country again. To satisfy his ambition and also to retaliate against England’s theft of his gold and silver, King Philip began to build his fleet of warships, the Spanish Armada, in January 1586.

Philip intended his fleet to be indestructible. In addition to building new warships, he marshaled 130 sailing vessels of all types and recruited more than 19,000 robust soldiers and 8,000 sailors. Although some of his ships lacked guns and others lacked ammunition, Philip was convinced that his Armada could withstand any battle with England.

The martial Armada set sail from Lisbon, Portugal, on May 9, 1588, but bad weather forced it back to port. The voyage resumed on July 22 after the weather became more stable.

The Spanish fleet met the smaller, faster, and more maneuverable English ships in battle off the coast of Plymouth, England, first on July 31 and again on August 2. The two battles left Spain vulnerable, having lost several ships and with its ammunition depleted. On August 7, while the Armada lay at anchor on the French side of the Strait of Dover, England sent eight burning ships into the midst of the Spanish fleet to set it on fire. Blocked on one side, the Spanish ships could only drift away, their crews in panic and disorder. Before the Armada could regroup, the English attacked again on August 8.

Although the Spaniards made a valiant effort to fight back, the fleet suffered extensive damage. During the eight hours of battle, the Armada drifted perilously close to the rocky coastline. At the moment when it seemed that the Spanish ships would be driven onto the English

shore, the wind shifted, and the Armada drifted out into the North Sea. The Spaniards recognized the superiority of the English fleet and returned home, defeated.

d. It aided Spanish regrouping in the North Sea.

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
Do you know the difference between a submarine and a submersible? A submarine is a watercraft capable of independent operation under the sea. Submarines do not require support ships because they can renew their air and power supplies independently. Submersibles also submerge and operate underwater, but they need the support of a larger vessel. Submersibles cannot renew their air and power supplies without support. For this reason, submersibles are usually smaller and cannot spend as much time underwater as submarines.

The first documented submersible was constructed in 1620 by Cornelius Drebbel. It was powered by rowing oars underwater. Though this craft was originally designed for underwater exploration, it did not take long for inventors and makers of war to recognize the military potential of the submersible. In 1648, Bishop John Wilkins wrote, “It may be of great advantage against a Navy of enemies, who by this may be undermined in the water and blown up.” Over one hundred years later, the first military submarine was ready to be deployed. The Turtle was the world’s first submarine used in combat. Designed by David Bushnell in 1775, it was deployed by the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. Though the Turtle did utilize a support ship in combat, it was fully capable of renewing its air and power supplies independently; therefore, the Turtle is considered to have

been a submarine and not a submersible. The Turtle was powered by hand-cranked propellers and was named as such because it resembled a turtle. It held a single person, moved about three miles per hour in calm water, and contained enough air to stay submerged for about thirty minutes.

General Washington authorized an attack using the Turtle on a British flagship blockading New York Harbor. Sgt. Ezra Lee operated the Turtle and attempted to affix underwater explosives to the British ship, but he failed. The Turtle was later destroyed by the British. Despite this failure, the Turtle is still remembered as the first submarine used offensively during war. Another notable submarine originally designed for war was Julius H. Kroehl’s Submarine Explorer. Built between 1863 and 1866, this submarine was created for the North during the American Civil War, but the war ended before it went into use. After the war, it was used commercially to harvest pearls in Panamanian waters during the late 1860s. Unfortunately, the dangers of decompression sickness (a condition that occurs when divers rise to the water’s surface too quickly) were not understood. While

experimenting with the Submarine Explorer in 1867, Kroehl himself perished from decompression sickness. In 1869, a new engineer put the Submarine Explorer back to the task of harvesting pearls.
Tragically, the use of the Submarine Explorer was discontinued after the entire crew died from decompression sickness. Submarine use increased greatly during World War I. Due to innovations in engineering, such as a dual power system using both diesel and electric sources, submarines had finally developed into effective war machines.

One watercraft called the U-Boat was put to great effect by the Germans. Some argue that the U-Boat was more of a submersible, since U-Boats operated primarily on the surface using diesel engines and submerged only occasionally to attack using battery power, but the effectiveness of the U-Boat in combat is certain. During World War I, more than 5,000 Allied ships were sunk by U- Boats, including the Lusitania, which is often cited as a reason why America entered the war. U- Boats were again utilized extensively by the Germans during World War II. Though the U-Boats were devastating to British fleets, advances in technology such as radar and sonar reduced their overall effectiveness. Additionally, the U.S. had also developed and deployed a fleet of submarines to great effect. Though the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor destroyed or severely damaged many of the U.S. Navy’s frontline Pacific Fleet ships, U.S. submarines survived the attack and went on to cause great damage. Submarines, though only about 2 percent of the U.S. Navy, destroyed over 30 percent of the Japanese Navy. This made U.S. submarines the most effective anti-ship and antisubmarine weapon in the entire American arsenal. Modern submarines are now powered by a nuclear reactor. The nuclear reactor generates a tremendous amount of power and frees the submarine from the need to occasionally

cards.text:
In 1892, the Sierra Club was formed. In 1908, an area of coastal redwood trees north of San Francisco was established as Muir Woods National Monument. In the Sierra Nevada Mountains, a walking trail from Yosemite Valley to Mount Whitney was dedicated in 1938. It is called the John Muir Trail.

John Muir was born in 1838 in Scotland. His family name means “moor,” which is a meadow full of flowers and animals. John loved nature from the time he was small. He also liked to climb rocky cliffs and walls. When John was 11 years old, his family moved to the United States and settled in Wisconsin. John was good with tools and soon became an inventor. He first invented a model of a sawmill. Later, he invented an alarm clock that would cause the sleeping person to be tipped out of bed when the timer sounded.

Muir left home at an early age. He took a 1,000-mile walk south to the Gulf of Mexico in 1867 and 1868. Then he sailed for San Francisco. The city was too noisy and crowded for Muir, so he headed inland for the Sierra Nevadas.

When Muir discovered the Yosemite Valley in the Sierra Nevadas, it was as if he had come home. He loved the mountains, the wildlife, and the trees. He climbed the mountains and even climbed trees during thunderstorms in order to get closer to the wind. He put forth the theory in the late 1860s that the Yosemite Valley had been formed through the action of glaciers. People ridiculed him. Not until 1930 was Muir’s theory proven correct.

Muir began to write articles about the Yosemite Valley to tell readers about its beauty. His writing also warned people that Yosemite was in danger from timber mining and sheep ranching interests. In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt became president of the United States. He was interested in conservation. Muir took the president through Yosemite, and Roosevelt helped get legislation passed to create Yosemite National Park in 1906.

Although Muir won many conservation battles, he lost a major one. He fought to save the Hetch Hetchy Valley, which people wanted to dam in order to provide water for San Francisco. In late 1913, a bill was signed to dam the valley. Muir died in 1914. Some people say losing the fight to protect the valley killed Muir.

●   State your opinion clearly.
●   Give one reason to support your opinion.

Example:
Topic: Is social media helping or harming students today?
I think social media is harming students today. Many students spend too much time on apps and games, which can make them tired and distracted from their studies. For example, some students scroll through social media instead of doing homework. Students should use social media less so it does not affect their learning.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: Write 3–4 sentences giving your opinion about whether the school cafeteria should offer more healthy snacks.

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
●   Start with a strong opinion (agree or disagree).
●   Give two reasons to support your viewpoint.
●   Provide one possible solution (e.g., limit, guidance).
●   End with a closing statement that urges readers to agree with you.
Example:
Social media is both helping and harming students, but I believe it is mostly harmful. It can help students communicate with friends and learn new things, but many spend too much time online, which affects their schoolwork and sleep. For example, students may stay up late watching videos instead of studying for tests. To reduce these problems, students should set limits on their social media use and focus on important tasks first. Schools and parents can also guide students to use social media responsibly. Using social media in moderation can help students enjoy its benefits without hurting their studies.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: Write a short editorial (1 paragraph).

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
Paragraph 1:

●   Present your opinion clearly.
●   Explain one positive and one negative effect of social media.
Paragraph 2:
●   State which effect you think is stronger and why.
●   Provide evidence or examples (realistic, simple ones).
●   End with a strong call to action (e.g., encouraging balanced or responsible use)
Example:
Social media is a powerful tool that can both help and harm students today.
On the positive side, it allows students to connect with classmates, share ideas, and access educational content online. For example, students can join study groups or watch tutorials on difficult topics. However, social media can also distract students, cause stress, and reduce the time they spend on homework or outdoor activities.
I believe the negative effects are stronger than the positive ones if social media is not used carefully. Students should be taught to use social media responsibly and set daily time limits. Parents and teachers can also encourage activities like reading, sports, or hobbies to balance screen time. By using social media wisely, students can enjoy its benefits without letting it harm their health or learning.

“River in Crisis: Plastic Waste Threatens Local Fish Population”
San Isidro, Laguna — Residents of Barangay Malinaw were shocked this week after local scientists released a report revealing dangerously high levels of plastic waste in the Maliit River, a waterway once known for its clear water and abundant fish.
According to the team of researchers from Laguna State Environmental Laboratory, plastic pollution in the river has increased by 63% in the last five years. The most concerning part of the study shows that if the trend continues, the community may lose up to 60% of its fish population in the next five years.
“We found plastic bags, sachets, straws, and even broken toys trapped in the riverbed,” said Dr. Elisa Ramos, lead scientist of the study. “Fish are mistaking microplastics for food. Many are getting sick or dying.”
Fisherfolk in the area have also noticed the alarming decline.
Mang Tonyo, a fisherman of 30 years, shared that his usual three kilos of fish per day has dropped to less than one kilo. “Minsan wala pa nga. Puno ng basura ang lambat namin,” he said, showing nets tangled with plastic waste.
Local officials admitted that the river cleanup programs have not been enough. Barangay Captain Lucia Hernandez urged residents to reduce single-use plastics and participate in the upcoming community clean-up next month.
Environmental groups warn that without immediate action, the river may become biologically dead—unable to support fish or other aquatic life.
“This river feeds families,” Dr. Ramos added. “If we lose it, we lose part of our community.”

Task:

●    Draw a cartoon showing how the river looks now, full of plastic waste.
●    Include fish, humans, and trash in a visual story:
o   Fish struggling or sick from microplastics. o   Mang Tonyo trying to catch fish in trash-filled nets. o   Residents or children holding signs: “Save Maliit River!”

“Luna and the Sad River”

In the town of Malinaw, there flowed a river that everyone loved. It was called the Maliit River, and it sparkled under the sun like a long, silver ribbon. Children played by its shore, fishermen caught fresh fish every morning, and families enjoyed picnics on weekends.
But one day, Luna, a curious 12-year-old girl, noticed something different.
When she sat by the river, she frowned.
“Why is the water… darker?” she whispered.
Instead of smooth stones and shiny fish, Luna saw plastic bags, sachets, straws, and even an old broken toy floating in the water.
The fish looked unhappy too. One small fish swam near her, bumping into bits of plastic.
“Oh no,” Luna said. “Are you okay?”
The fish couldn’t speak, of course, but Luna imagined it saying, “We’re trying… but the trash is making it hard to breathe.”
That afternoon, Luna went to visit Mang Tonyo, the friendly fisherman who always told funny stories. She saw him pulling up his fishing net, but instead of fish, it was full of plastic.
“Mang Tonyo, what happened?” Luna asked.
He sighed. “The river is sick, anak. There’s too much trash. I used to catch three kilos of fish every day. Now… sometimes I catch none.”
Luna felt a tight squeeze in her chest. How could a river get sick?
The next day at school, Dr. Ramos, a scientist from the community, visited their class.
“Children,” she said gently, “we studied the Maliit River, and we found that plastic waste has increased a lot. If nothing changes, we might lose more than half of the fish in just a few years.”

The whole class gasped.
“But it’s not too late,” Dr. Ramos continued with a hopeful smile. “If we work together, we can help the river heal.”
Luna’s eyes brightened. She had an idea.
That weekend, with help from her classmates, she organized a River Rescue Day. They brought gloves, sacks, and posters that said, “A Clean River is a Happy River!” Even parents and neighbors joined in.
They picked up trash, sorted recyclables, and planted new plants along the riverbank. It was hard work, but Luna felt proud.
At the end of the day, she sat by the river again. This time, she saw something wonderful—small fish swimming freely in a cleaner spot.
Luna smiled.
“Don’t worry, little river,” she whispered. “We’re here to help.”
And from that day on, the people of Malinaw promised to take better care of the Maliit River—so it could sparkle once more and stay alive for future generations.

Task:

●    Draw a cartoon showing Luna discovering the polluted river.
●    Include:
o   Dark, plastic-filled water o   Sad or struggling fish o   Luna’s worried expression

●    Optional: A thought bubble for the fish: “We’re trying… but the trash is making it hard to breathe.”

Example: Title: A Day in the Life of Mrs. Gomez, Our Cafeteria Manager Mrs. Gomez unlocks the cafeteria door at 6:30 a.m., long before most of the students arrive. She pushes a heavy cart filled with trays, cleaning supplies, and fresh bread. “I always like to start early,” she says, smiling. “I want everything to be ready when the kids come in.” By 7:00, she’s already busy: setting up breakfast stations, warming up the ovens, and arranging milk cartons. She hums softly as she works, greeting the first students with a friendly “Good morning!” She knows many of them by name and asks how their morning is going or what they think of the new menu. During lunch, Mrs. Gomez doesn’t just serve food — she listens. A student once told her they didn’t like any sandwiches, so she helped make a special salad just for them. “If I can make someone happy with food, then I feel like I’ve done something good,” she says. Read the editorial “It’s Time to Modernize Our School Dress Code.” After reading, carefully analyze the writer’s stand, arguments, and overall structure. Then, answer the guide questions provided below in complete sentences. Make sure your answers show your understanding of how editorial writing presents opinions, supports claims with reasons, and encourages readers to take action.

It’s Time to Modernize Our School Dress Code School dress codes are meant to promote discipline and unity, but our current policy no longer reflects the needs of today’s students. While rules are important, some parts of the dress code have become outdated, uncomfortable, and unfair. It is time for the school to update and modernize the policy to create a more inclusive environment.
First, some of the restrictions no longer match modern clothing trends.
Students are often reprimanded for wearing outfits that are common, appropriate, and comfortable for everyday use. This not only embarrasses students but also disrupts their learning. Instead of focusing on small details like sleeve length or hair accessories, the dress code should focus on what truly matters: comfort, safety, and respect.
Second, certain rules tend to affect some students more than others.
For example, girls are more frequently disciplined for minor dress code issues, which can make them feel judged or singled out. A modernized dress code should be fair and equal, avoiding rules that target specific groups. A clearer, gender-neutral policy would make the school feel more supportive for everyone.
Finally, updating the dress code can help students feel more confident.
When students are comfortable with what they wear, they are more likely to participate in class and stay focused. A simple change in policy can lead to a more positive school atmosphere.
Updating the dress code doesn’t mean removing rules—it means improving them. Our school has the chance to create a policy that respects both tradition and the needs of today’s learners. By revising the dress code, we can promote fairness, comfort, and confidence for all students. It’s time to make the change.

cards.text: 1. Pick a Social Media Trend or Issue o     Choose a trend, challenge, or issue related to social media that is relevant to teenagers: mental health, “cancel culture,” misinformation, viral challenges, body image, privacy, digital activism, etc.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 2. Research o     Find data, news stories, and real-life examples about your topic. o     Interview at least two people: classmates, teachers, or someone in your community who has an opinion or experience with this trend or issue.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 3. Plan Your Feature o     Use a graphic organizer to outline: ▪   A hook (a surprising fact, a personal story, or a question) ▪   Background / context ▪   Real-life stories / quotes from your interviews ▪   A reflection or call to action: Why should people care? What can be done?

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 4. Write Your Feature Article o     Write a 5-paragraph feature: ▪   Lead: Start with an anecdote or fact related to the trend ▪   Body 1: Explain the trend / issue (what it is, how it started) ▪   Body 2: Share stories or impact (quotes from interviews) ▪   Body 3: Discuss positive and negative effects / complexities ▪   Conclusion: Reflect on what the trend means for you and your peers propose a solution, raise a question, or call to action. Example: Title: The Invisible Weight: Social Media and Teen Mental Health Lead (Paragraph 1): Every night around 10 PM, 15-year-old Kayla opens TikTok, swipes through a stream of dance videos, beauty tutorials, and vloggers talking about their “glow-up” journeys. She pauses on a clip where a popular creator talks about how they feel “not good enough” without filters. “Sometimes I feel like that too,” Kayla says quietly. For many teenagers, the glow of their phone screen doesn’t just light up their room — it also lights up insecurities. Body 1 (Explaining the Trend): social media plays a huge role in teenage life today. According to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, 45% of teens say they spend too much time on social media — a number that’s risen steadily in recent years. While many teens say these platforms help them feel more connected (74%) or creative (63%), others admit there’s a cost: nearly 1 in 5 say social media hurts their mental health. At the same time, a World Health Organization report found that about 11% of adolescents show signs of problematic social media use — struggling to control their usage and feeling negative consequences. Body 2 (Stories & Impact): To understand how this plays out in real life, I spoke with two classmates, Marco and Jess. Marco, 16, says his TikTok notifications are a “double- edged sword.” “When I get a lot of likes I feel proud, but when I don’t, I question why I even posted,” he says. Jess, 14, says Instagram is a place for both connection and competition. “I follow people who seem to have perfect lives — but when I compare, I feel small,” she admits. Their experiences reflect a bigger pattern: that behind every “like” or share is often a struggle with self-worth. Body 3 (Complexities — Positives & Negatives): social media isn’t all bad. Many teens use it as a place for self-expression, community, and even healing. In the same Pew survey, 34% of teens said they sometimes get mental health information from these platforms — and of those, 63% say it’s an important source. But the negatives are real, too. According to the Mayo Clinic, what teens do on social media matters: viewing content about self-harm, unrealistic beauty standards, or risky behavior can increase anxiety and low self-esteem. Experts suggest that moderation may be key — because using social media doesn’t necessarily have to be harmful, but overuse or exposure to certain content can be. Conclusion (Reflection / Call to Action): So what can we, as teens, do about this? First, we can set healthier boundaries — limit screen time, mute stressful accounts, and take “digital detox” breaks. Second, we can support each other: talk openly when we feel the pressure of comparison or when social media messes with our self- esteem. And finally, we can push for a change: schools can host workshops about healthy social media habits, and we can encourage creators to show real life — not just the highlight reel. If we learn to use social media with purpose, maybe we can make it a place that builds us up — instead of weighing us down.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 5. Write Your Draft Write a 4- or 5-paragraph feature article: ▪   Paragraph 1 (Lead): Open with a scene, personal story, or fact that highlights the environmental issue. ▪   Paragraph 2: Explain what the problem is, with data / background. ▪   Paragraph 3: Include voices from your interviews — real people, quotes, personal impact. ▪   Paragraph 4: Describe current efforts or possible solutions. ▪   Paragraph 5 (Conclusion): Reflect on why this issue matters and suggest a call-to-action or hope for change. Example: Title: Sachets, Streets, and the Sea: How Plastic Pollution Affects Our Community Paragraph 1 (Lead): On a typical morning, 14-year-old Mia walks beside the small creek that winds behind her neighborhood. She used to toss snack wrappers and empty sachet packets on the ground — “they’re small,” she would say, “they’ll just disappear.” But now, she pauses. The creek is no longer clear: she sees bits of colorful plastic bobbing on the surface. “When I was younger, I never thought my trash could end up in the sea,” she admits. Paragraph 2 (Background / Problem): Plastic pollution is a massive problem in the Philippines. According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), about 24% of the country’s daily 61,000 metric tons of solid waste is plastic. Every year, the Philippines generates around 2.7 million metric tons of plastic waste, much of which ends up in landfills, rivers, or the ocean. Single-use plastics, like sachets, are especially problematic — they don’t biodegrade, they break down into microplastics, and they contribute to flooding by clogging drainage systems. Paragraph 3 (Voices / Stories): I spoke with Mr. Navarro, a barangay (village) official, who says, “Plastic waste isn’t just dirty — it’s dangerous.” He explained that clogged waterways during the rainy season make flooding worse, especially when heavy rains come. I also met Marisol; a local youth volunteer who helps organize barangay cleanups. “We collect plastic sachets every weekend,” she told me. “It’s heartbreaking to see how many people don’t bother to put trash in bins.” Paragraph 4 (Solutions / Efforts): There are hopeful signs. In 2025, the government launched the National Plastic Action Partnership (NPAP) to address plastic waste with stronger collaboration among communities, businesses, and government agencies. At the local level, students in Mia’s school started a “Plastic to Purpose” drive: they collect used sachets, sort them, and send them to a recycling center. For the microplastics that don’t get recycled, they’re talking to barangay officials about installing filters in the creek to trap litter before it reaches the sea. Paragraph 5 (Reflection / Call to Action): Mia now thinks twice before throwing anything out. “I realized my small actions matter,” she says. But she also knows that change isn’t just on her shoulders. We — as a school and a community — need to act. We can reduce single-use plastics, support local cleanups, and pressure companies to package products responsibly. If enough of us do something, maybe one day, the creek won’t be plastic-filled, and our streets won’t feed our seas.

(e.g., a personal story, a surprising fact) ▪   Body: Key points data, personal stories, interviews ▪   Reflection / Solutions: What can be done, or what hope do people have ▪   Conclusion: A strong closing thought that ties back to your hook

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 5. Write Your Draft sWrite a 4- or 5-paragraph feature article: ▪   Lead / Opening – Begin with a story, anecdote, or strong fact about poverty in your area. ▪   Body Paragraph 1 – Explain the issue using your research / data. ▪   Body Paragraph 2 – Include voices from your interviews — what people said, their experiences. ▪   Body Paragraph 3 (if you do 5 paragraphs) – Talk about current efforts, programs, or possible solutions. ▪   Conclusion – Reflect on why the issue matters, what you learned, and a call to action or hopeful message. Example: Title: Invisible Yet Real: The Hidden Struggles of Middle-Income Families Paragraph 1 (Lead): From the outside, the Ramos family’s home looks like any other in North Quezon City — a tidy two-storey house, a small car in the driveway, and children running out to play. But inside, Mama Luz worries every month: “We don’t make much more than what we spent two decades ago,” she confides. Her husband’s salary barely keeps up with rising costs, and for many people, they are “just about getting by.” Paragraph 2 (Background / Issue): While “poverty” often conjures images of extreme hardship, there is a growing number of working poor families — those whose income is above the poverty line but still isn’t enough to cover all basic needs or cushion emergencies. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, income thresholds to meet basic needs (food and non-food) are rising. For 2023, a five-member family needed about ₱13,873/month. Even though the national poverty rate has dropped to 15.5% in 2023, many families feel the squeeze from inflation, medical costs, and school fees. Paragraph 3 (Voices / Stories): I talked to Luz’s son, Dante, a Grade 9 student: “Sometimes I skip snack money so my little sister can eat.” His older sister, Maribel, is working part- time in a coffee shop. She says, “I pay for my own school supplies, but Mum worries about paying rent if something happens.” Their mother adds that she sometimes hesitates to ask for help — pride and stigma make it hard for her to acknowledge their struggle. Paragraph 4 (Current Efforts / Possible Solutions): Some communities are responding: a local church in their area started a “Community Care Fund” where residents contribute a small amount each month to help others pay for utilities or school fees. There’s also a non-profit that provides financial literacy training so families can budget better and save more. But Luz believes these efforts must be expanded: “More people need to know about help, and it must be easier to apply.” Paragraph 5 (Reflection / Call to Action): The Ramos family’s story reminds us that poverty isn’t always obvious — it can hide in homes that look “fine” on the outside. As classmates and friends, we need to challenge what we think poverty looks like. Schools can offer workshops on financial literacy or partner with local NGOs. We can also support policies that help all working families, not just those at the very bottom. Because when we see more clearly, we can help more meaningfully.

8:10:104:1.instruction: Read the editorial carefully. Analyze the writer’s stand, arguments, evidence, and overall structure. Then, answer the guide questions in complete sentences. Focus on how the editorial presents opinions, supports claims, addresses counterarguments, and persuades readers to take action.

cards.title: Read
cards.text:
Should Schools Adopt a Later Start Time?

Many high school students struggle with fatigue, poor concentration, and declining mental health, largely because school starts too early.
Research shows that teenagers have different sleep cycles than adults and naturally stay up later at night. It is time for schools to adopt later start times to improve students’ health, academic performance, and overall well- being.

First, early school hours negatively impact students’ physical and mental health. Sleep deprivation can lead to stress, anxiety, poor immunity, and reduced cognitive functioning. By starting school later, students are more likely to get the recommended 8–10 hours of sleep, leading to better mood, energy, and focus in class.

Second, academic performance improves when students are well- rested. Studies indicate that schools with later start times have higher attendance rates, better test scores, and increased engagement in lessons.
When students are alert, they can absorb and retain information more effectively, resulting in stronger academic outcomes.

Some argue that changing the start time may interfere with after- school activities, sports, and parental schedules. While adjustments are necessary, the benefits of better sleep and mental health far outweigh the logistical challenges. Schools can modify schedules gradually or provide flexible extracurricular timings to accommodate students and families.

In conclusion, shifting school start times is a simple yet powerful way to support teenagers’ physical health, mental well-being, and academic success. Educators, parents, and policymakers must work together to make this change. It’s time to prioritize students’ needs and give them the rest they deserve.

Step-by-Step Instructions:

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 1. Choose a subject: Select a person in your school or community whose daily life or experiences are interesting. Examples: a teacher, a school staff member, a local artist, or a peer with a unique hobby.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 2. Plan your approach: Think of 5–7 questions to ask during an interview, focusing on their daily routine, challenges, achievements, and personal interests.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 3. Observe: Spend time observing your subject in their environment. Take detailed notes about their actions, expressions, and interactions.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 4. Conduct an interview: Use your prepared questions. Record or write down their responses verbatim to include direct quotes in your article.

cards.title: Write
cards.text: 5. Write your feature article (400–500 words): o    Lead: Begin with an engaging anecdote or scene from their day. o    Body: Share their story, including quotes, descriptive details, and personal insights. o    Conclusion: Reflect on what makes this person’s life inspiring, interesting, or unique. EXAMPLE: Mr. Daniel, the school janitor Lead: Every morning at 5:30 a.m., while most of the town is still asleep, Mr. Daniel is already sweeping the empty corridors of Riverside High School. The faint smell of disinfectant fills the air as he hums a soft tune, preparing the school for another day of learning. Body: Mr. Daniel has worked at Riverside High for over 15 years. “I enjoy seeing the students smile when the school is clean,” he says with a warm grin. His day begins with sweeping and mopping floors, followed by restocking classrooms and checking that all facilities are in order. Despite his busy schedule, he always finds time to greet students by name. “It’s the small things that make my day worthwhile,” he explains. Outside work, Mr. Daniel volunteers at the local community center, helping children with homework and organizing weekend sports activities. Conclusion: Mr. Daniel’s dedication reminds everyone that every role in the school community matters. Through his hard work and kindness, he quietly makes Riverside High a brighter place for students and staff alike.

EXAMPLE: DIY Resin Art Lead: Over the past year, a colorful wave of creativity has taken over social media: DIY resin art. From glittery keychains to miniature landscapes, teenagers are turning their free time into artistic masterpieces. Body: Resin art involves mixing resin with pigments, glitter, and molds to create small decorative items. Teens like 16-year-old Maya explain why they love it: “It’s relaxing, and I love seeing the final product shine.” The trend has gained attention on Instagram and TikTok, with thousands of posts under #ResinArt. Schools and online communities now host workshops where beginners can learn to craft their own resin pieces. Experts note that resin art encourages creativity and patience, giving teenagers a productive way to spend their time. Impact: While resin art is mostly positive, some teens spend large amounts on supplies, which can be costly. However, many view it as a hobby that boosts confidence and skills. Conclusion: From glitter-filled coasters to custom jewelry, DIY resin art shows how a simple craft can inspire a generation of young creators. As more teens experiment with colors and shapes, the trend is likely to grow even further.

cards.text: 6. Revise and proofread: Ensure your article flow well, has correct grammar, and creates a; strong impression of the location. Example: Maple Grove Park Lead: Tucked behind the main road in downtown Oakville, Maple Grove Park is a serene escape from the city’s hustle. The soft rustling of leaves and the scent of blooming flowers greet visitors as they step onto winding cobblestone paths. Body: The Park is dotted with wooden benches, perfect for reading or quiet reflection. Children play near the small fountain, while joggers circle the walking trails. “I come here every morning; it’s peaceful and refreshing,” says local resident Mr. Cruz. Historically, Maple Grove Park was established in 1920 and still retains its century-old oak trees. Birdsong fills the air, and butterflies often flutter past the flowerbeds, adding to the park’s charm. Conclusion: Whether you’re seeking a quiet spot to read, a place to exercise, or a peaceful escape from the busy city, Maple Grove Park is a hidden gem worth exploring. It proves that sometimes, the most beautiful places are the ones we least expect.
